No one has been able to repeat the success of these books, because it wasn't just a girl went saw a bunch of crazy stuff. Lewis Carol was a mathematician and there is a subtext of mathematics throughout the books. http://www.ams.org/news/math-in-the-media/mmarc-02-2010-media https://www.maa.org/external_archive/devlin/devlin_03_10.html http://www.nytimes.com/2010/03/07/opinion/07bayley.html?pagewanted=all&_r=0

I heard in school that the books weren't so much the fanciful rantings of a pedophile trying to seduce his prey as much as a mathematician ranting against the contemporary "new math." Either one is still interesting in and of its own right.

There are plenty of reasons for the popularity of both books. I can offer a few; there are others who can add more. It's difficult to give a complete answer in the space provided here.

First, the books are highly imaginative in a silly putty elastic way. This is certainly conveyed through the language, but it is also evident from the numerous illustrations which accompany the story.

Second, the story is episodic so it is not only easy to read, but it can be dropped at one moment and picked up later without much disruption to the flow of the story.

Lastly, the episodes are surreal. The dream like state that Carroll creates is a joyful roller coaster ride of things that look familiar but don't make alot of sense. Anyone who has taken drugs like LSD or smoked grass probably has had an enhanced experience reading the books.

Oh, yes. The books are humorous, too.

I can't speak to how popular they were when they were published but no doubt a certain amount of their enduring popularity is due to the Disney film.

I'm reasonably sure that many classics are largely only remembered because of Disney. Would many (any?) of us have even heard of Mary Poppins, Dumbo, even Peter Pan without those wonderful Disney treatments?
